text.intro:
Work on the analysis items of the AAAR master to-do list (email to Ann, 22 Oct). Unless stated otherwise:
the 189 Addis filters on the poster; spline baseline-corrected spectra (1425–4000 cm⁻¹); Deming fits of FTIR EC
against HIPS EC (Fabs / MAC 10) with the poster's error ratio. The season-specific calibrations are Figure 9's,
refitted here and checked to reproduce it exactly. Code: `research/ftir_hips_chem/workflows/run_meeting_20261028.py`.

**What we found**

- **Choose by chemistry, not spectral shape.** The 500 IMPROVE filters with the lowest TOR OC/EC fix most of Belg
   (0.32x +1.06 (R² 0.22) becomes 0.72x -1.16 (R² 0.61)) and help Dry a
   little. The six urban IMPROVE sites give nearly the same result. Kiremt does worse than with its spectral
   look-alikes, and no selection gets Dry near slope 1.
- **Within Dry and Belg, the filters with the least organic signal are read lowest** (partial ρ
   0.46 and 0.63). Kiremt shows no
   such link (0.09). This supports the organic-deficit explanation.
- **It is not dust, MAC, or TOR on dark filters.** Dust/EC is the same in every season. Slope 1 would need a MAC of
   28–32 in Dry and Belg. OP-zero IMPROVE
   filters have lower, not higher, TOR/HIPS.
- **Loading explains part of it.** Out-of-range IMPROVE filters read about 0.74 of TOR, while Addis reads
   0.30 of HIPS at the same loading.
- **The raw (SPARTAN) calibration leans on background and dust regions** (30% of VIP² below 1425 cm⁻¹,
   18% at 3600–4000). The 3600–4000 cm⁻¹ residual at Addis tracks dust (Si), not sulfate.
- **Kiremt's higher EC is mostly a shallower boundary layer.** Per column of air, Kiremt has no more EC than Dry
   (0.83 of Dry).
text.ocec:
**Choosing the calibration filters by chemistry helps Belg most, Dry a little, and costs Kiremt some of its
Figure 9 gain.** Addis OC/EC (SPARTAN OC over HIPS EC) has a median of 0.55 in Dry,
0.63 in Belg and 0.87 in Kiremt. Only 0.5% of the IMPROVE filters
with at least 1 µg of EC have an OC/EC below 1 (median 5.3). So the filters "nearest Addis" are simply
the lowest-OC/EC filters in IMPROVE (median 1.78, from 116 sites), and one set
serves every season. The table below the chart has every fit.

- **Belg** moves from 0.32x +1.06 (R² 0.22) to 0.72x -1.16 (R² 0.61): the
  positive intercept is gone and R² nearly triples.
- **Dry** improves only in slope (0.35 to
  0.50). It stays the worst season under every selection.
- **Kiremt** does worse than with its own spectral look-alikes (0.94
  to 0.75).
- The **six urban IMPROVE sites** (Atlanta, Birmingham, Fresno, Phoenix, Pittsburgh, Seattle (Puget Sound); median OC/EC 3.2,
  630 filters) give almost the same answer as the low-OC/EC set, and predict their own sites well
  (leave-one-site-out TOR R² 0.69).
- Combining both (the 2,000 most spectrally similar, then the 500 with the lowest OC/EC) lands in between.

Both chemistry-based sets also predict held-out IMPROVE better than the spectral look-alikes (TOR R²
0.79 vs 0.42
to 0.60). No selection reaches slope 1 in Dry.
text.deficit:
**Yes, in Dry and Belg; not in Kiremt.** For each Addis filter, the organic signal is the C–H, O–H and
carbonyl band areas (baseline-corrected, per m³, averaged as percentiles). The test is the partial Spearman
correlation between FTIR EC and that signal, with HIPS EC held fixed, so a positive value means filters with more
organic material per unit EC are read higher.

- Season-specific calibrations (Figure 9): Dry 0.46,
  Belg 0.63, Kiremt 0.09.
- SPARTAN's published EC shows the same pattern (Dry 0.33,
  Belg 0.39, Kiremt -0.14).

So within Dry and Belg the filters with the least organic signal for their EC are the ones read lowest, as the
organic-deficit explanation predicts. In Kiremt, which already carries the most organic signal per unit EC
(21 Oct notebook), the error no longer depends on it. This is a correlation within 51–73 filters per season, not
a proof of mechanism.
text.dust:
**Dust does not explain Dry and Belg.** Dust relative to EC is about the same in every season
(Si/EC 0.25–0.28, Al/EC 0.07–0.09). Kiremt
actually has the most dust in absolute terms (Si 1.56 µg/m³ vs 1.06 in Dry).
With HIPS EC held fixed, more dust goes with slightly *lower* FTIR EC in every season and calibration (partial ρ
-0.50 to -0.15). The strongest link is SPARTAN's published EC in Kiremt
(-0.50). Note that the
baseline-corrected spectra stop at 1425 cm⁻¹, so the Si-O band near 1035 cm⁻¹ is not in those calibrations at all.
Only the raw (SPARTAN) calibration sees it.
text.mac:
**MAC does not explain it either.** HIPS EC is Fabs / 10 in every season. The IMPROVE look-alikes' own
ratio of Fabs to TOR EC is close to 10 (Dry 11.7, Belg
11.4, Kiremt 9.8 m²/g).
Using it instead of 10 moves the season-specific slopes only a little (Dry 0.35 to
0.41). Reaching slope 1 would need a MAC of
28 in Dry and 32 in Belg, two to three times
any plausible value. Kiremt would need 10.7. As expected, the intercepts do not
change with MAC.
text.highwn:
**The 3600–4000 cm⁻¹ residual tracks dust, not sulfate.** After baseline correction, Addis keeps some
absorbance above 3600 cm⁻¹. Within every season it follows SPARTAN Si closely (Spearman ρ Dry 0.83,
Belg 0.90, Kiremt 0.89). It follows sulfate only weakly
(0.13, 0.19, 0.49), and goes down, not up, with
humidity. So it looks like scattering by mineral dust rather than the sulfate-related scattering Anwar (2025)
describes. Kiremt, where this residual is largest relative to its look-alikes (21 Oct notebook), is also the
dustiest season.
text.loading:
**Loading explains part of it, not most.** PLS underpredicts heavy filters even within IMPROVE. On
held-out IMPROVE sites the median FTIR/TOR ratio falls from 1.00 at 5–10 µg EC to
0.79 at 20–40 µg. A calibration trained only on filters below
20 µg, predicting the 367 heavier ones, reads 0.74 of TOR at 20–40 µg and
0.68 at 40–80 µg.

At the same 20–40 µg the baseline-corrected calibration reads Addis at 0.30 of HIPS. So out-of-range
loading costs IMPROVE about a quarter of its EC, while Addis loses about two thirds; loading is part of the story,
and composition is the larger part. SPARTAN's raw calibration reads Addis at
0.86 at 20–40 µg and
1.31 at 40–80 µg. It overshoots as loading rises, which is
the steep slope in Figure 4.
text.dark:
**No sign that TOR EC runs high on dark IMPROVE filters.** Where optical pyrolysis reads zero
(2.9% of the library), TOR EC relative to HIPS/10 is *lower*, not higher, than on other
filters at the same loading (2–5 µg: 0.68 vs 0.98; 5–10 µg: 0.69
vs 0.92). The look-alikes are rarely OP-zero filters (none of the 97; 0.2%
of Dry's, 9.8% of Kiremt's). One thing to keep in mind: above 20 µg, TOR runs above
HIPS/10 in IMPROVE (1.14 at 20–40 µg, 1.81 above 40). If Addis TOR behaved the
same way, Addis TOR EC would be higher than HIPS/10, and the FTIR shortfall against TOR would be larger, not smaller.
text.vip:
**The raw (SPARTAN-like) calibration reads EC from different parts of the spectrum than the
baseline-corrected ones.** VIP² shares by region:

- Raw: 30% below 1425 cm⁻¹ (PTFE 10%), 18% at
  3600–4000, and only 7% on C–H and 19% on O–H.
- Baseline-corrected, all IMPROVE: 41% O–H, 23% C–H,
  21% carbonyl.

Section 5 found that the 3600–4000 cm⁻¹ region carries Addis dust scattering. So the raw calibration leans on the
regions where Addis differs from IMPROVE in background and dust, not in EC. That is a plausible reason it overshoots
on heavy Addis filters (Section 6). The baseline-corrected calibrations lean on the organic bands, which Addis has
little of per unit EC. Kiremt's look-alike calibration puts the most weight on C–H
(35%); the low-OC/EC set puts the most on carbonyl
(23%).
text.speciation:
**Addis is EC-rich and organic-poor next to every IMPROVE group, including its own look-alikes.** Median
shares of PM2.5:

- EC is 19%–24% at Addis against
  4%–8% in the look-alikes.
- OC is 13%–16% against
  18%–31%.
- OC/EC is 0.55–0.87 against
  3.6–4.7.
- Soil is a bigger share at Addis (21%–26%).
- Sulfate is a smaller share, except that Dry's look-alikes are sulfate-rich (21%).
- The urban IMPROVE sites are the closest IMPROVE group in OC/EC (3.2) and in
  EC share (8%).

Caveat: Addis OC is SPARTAN's FTIR OC and Addis EC is HIPS/10; IMPROVE OC and EC are TOR. Soil uses the IMPROVE
formula on SPARTAN elements.
text.blh:
**Kiremt's higher concentrations are mostly a shallower boundary layer.** The ERA5 boundary-layer height,
averaged over each filter's sampling window, has a median of 687 m in Dry,
525 m in Belg and 407 m in Kiremt.
Concentrations relative to Dry, before and after multiplying by the boundary-layer height:

- HIPS EC: 1.30 becomes 0.83.
- PM2.5: 1.69 becomes 1.03.
- OC: 2.05 becomes 1.21.

So per column of air there is no more EC in Kiremt than in Dry. OC stays somewhat higher, which fits more smoke
in Kiremt. The boundary-layer height says little about the calibration error: with HIPS EC held fixed, its partial
correlation with the season-specific FTIR EC is -0.34
in Dry and near zero in Belg and Kiremt. (Concentration × boundary-layer height is a rough column measure: one
surface site, and the height averaged over each filter's window.)
text.next:
- **Build calibration sets from chemistry and spectra together.** For example, low OC/EC and urban sites
  as the base, with the heaviest filters added, then read the result on Dry with repeated site splits (not one split).
- **Test whether the organic deficit is the cause, not just a correlation.** Add organic absorbance to the IMPROVE
  filters, or take it away from Addis, and see whether the Addis prediction moves as expected.
- **Pull the raw calibration off the background regions.** Refit it on raw spectra without 3600–4000 cm⁻¹ and
  without the region below 1425, and see whether the Addis slope drops toward 1 without baseline correction.
- **Loading:** a calibration that includes the heavy IMPROVE filters (≥ 20 µg), or weights them up.
- **Before relying on the OC/EC result:** Addis OC is SPARTAN's FTIR OC. Check it against the Addis city TOR
  filters when they arrive.
